title: Meditation and Memory with Anthony Metivier

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Welcome to Deconstructing Yourself, the podcast for metamodern mutants interested in meditation, awakening, Vajrayana, tantra, Shaivism, non-duality, consciousness hacking, and much more. My name is Michael Taft, your host on the podcast, and in this episode I'm speaking with Anthony Metivier. Anthony Metivier is the founder of the Magnetic Memory Method, a modern systematic approach to memorizing foreign language vocabulary, names, music, poetry, sacred texts, and more. Dr. Metivier holds a Ph.D. in Humanities from York University and is widely known for his books, talks, and courses on memory improvement. And without further ado, I give you the episode that I call Memory and Meditation with Anthony Metivier.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Anthony, welcome to the Deconstructing Yourself podcast.

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: So great to speak with you, Michael. I've seen your stuff or listened to it, and you're a shining light, really. I aspire to have so much clarity about these matters as you have, and maybe get there one day.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Thanks. I often feel like I'm just a mass of confusion, so that's very sweet of you to say that, and I appreciate it. My experience is that I got introduced to you not that long ago, and I was just blown away. So listening to your three different episodes on Guru Viking, I was impressed because all three of them were interesting to me. And I was like, wow, this is really cool what this guy is into, the way you're working with memory and the science of memory and helping people to memorize much more effectively, how that can fit into spiritual practice, even in terms of just sharpening our concentration, you know, kind of increasing our ability to stay with certain topics. But beyond that, memorizing sacred texts and even reciting them, which is something I'm particularly into and excited about. And then also even more deep and powerful and maybe not exclusive to the meditation or spiritual practice realm is learning of foreign languages, but in this case, like ancient languages of various spiritual practice traditions. So all of this just really lit me up. I was like, wow, this guy is really doing some cool stuff. So hopefully we can unpack some of that a little more fully here today.

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: That'd be great. Yeah, absolutely. It's always fun to talk about these things.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Great. So how did you get into this memory stuff, Anthony? It's kind of an odd thing to be fully preoccupied with. It's unusual, right? It's not that many people go down the deep end there.

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: Yeah, although there may be more than it seems. The way I got into it was just a blessing of circumstance, and I'll try to give the compressed version, but the early origins is that I was really in trouble in grad school, and I almost didn't finish grad school because of psychiatric issues. And, you know, it was the kind of thing with hospitalization and pills, and I was very beholden to science, and I don't think incorrectly necessarily, but I tried those programs. But the problem with taking certain medicines was literally that I would start to drool and I couldn't focus on anything. And that just made the depression worse. So I was at campus one day, and at York University there's a little place called York Lanes, which kind of like makes a street look like it's indoors. And I was walking through there and this magician came and showed me a trick. And this was when street magic was all the rage. And basically I got super interested in magic because I'd done it as a kid. And in magic I found the holy grail of tricks, which is called any card at any number. And I just thought, well, this is better than sitting around being depressed and, you know, not being able to focus on a page of French theory. And YouTube was new at the time, so I could watch what these magicians were doing. Anyway, this idea came of any card at any number, and to do it well you basically have to know the deck inside and out. And there's various stack orders that people use. I've used the Mnemonica stack or the Redford stack. There's just really wild stuff going on there. And I found that I actually could follow the instructions and memorize the deck. And I instantly thought, man, if I can do this, I can get weird terms like architectonic tautology into memory. And that's what I did. And at least a decade and a half before I ever saw any research on the use of memory palaces, which is what I used to memorize the cards, I started to feel better. Not cured of depression, not suddenly off medication, but just better. And I thought it was just kind of strange, but I went with it. And then I think it was about 15 years later I read the Tim Dalgleish research — and it's Tim Dalgleish et al, with his co-researchers. Anyway, he studied method of loci, which is another term for memory palace, with people who have depression, people who have PTSD, and he found that if they use these techniques they do feel better, they have more robustness for dealing with things that come up in these conditions. But then how I got into teaching it, that was another sort of strange accident. I was unemployed for some time, near homelessness, and I had a kind of weird job at an after-school school, the kind of place that you see on streets where parents send their kids after school so that they get a proper education, so to speak. And I was writing curricula, and a teacher didn't show up, and so the owner of that school asked me to go in there and teach them. So I did, and I just got through the stuff very quickly. I said, what do you want to do next? And they said, if we don't know, you're the teacher. So I said, let's learn to memorize the alphabet backwards. I taught them that stunt and they asked me to write it down, and I did. And the Kindle gold mine was happening at the time, and I just — long story short, I put a version of what I wrote for them onto the internet and it became a bestseller. And I just thought, well, if I can do that, I mean, let's go. And so that's what I did. And I never stopped.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So did you find that your initial foray into memorizing the deck of cards and then working on your grad school stuff, did your experience reproduce what the researchers showed about how memorizing stuff actually increases your feeling of resource and robustness? Did it help you feel better?

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: Well, it did literally make me feel better, but I may be having some backward reasoning. I don't know. I mean, it's kind of like confirmation bias. Wow, here's this thing. But to be fair, I was at that time — part of my research that I did as a grad student and I wrote my dissertation on was on friendship. And in friendship, I was studying hypnosis. So I also had some self-hypnosis things that I was doing at the time. And also I wasn't that super serious about it at the time, but I did have a very bare bones meditative practice. In my case, there isn't sort of this single origin story, you know, there's so many things going on. And I often worry when I give interviews and tell these stories because of what I know about memory, and this is reflected in the research of people giving testimony at court, how easily we change our own memories by accessing them. So, you know, I think Jacques Lacan said there's just too many words, you know, to ever tell the truth. So at the end of the day, something happened, that's for sure. And I could speculate all kinds of wild things, like, oh, I connected with our deep ancestral techniques, which, you know, is true, these are very ancient techniques, or I did this or I did that. But at the end of the day, whatever happened, I was able to go and sit for my field examinations and not be bowled over, because there's some very mean people at some of these examinations. And I was able to just — I remember, and this is again my memory, so it may not have happened exactly this way, but I remember being attacked in my dissertation defense: where is the Nietzsche in your dissertation? And I just pushed the document forward and I tapped it. I said, page 72. I might have messed the grammar up there a little bit, but, you know, it says you can never adorn yourself enough for your friends, so you must be like a longing and an arrow for him. And that sort of stopped the argument about there being no Nietzsche in my dissertation. So it didn't feel good to do that, it actually felt bad, but I felt good enough that I could do that. Like there was this confidence and this clarity of tracking the examination and then just knowing what I was in my own writing, and that came from actually memorizing that line. And this is just a kind of example.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's so interesting. Were you always good at memorizing stuff? Let's say before you started having a mental health crisis, did you have an exceptional memory to begin with?

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: I don't know that I did or didn't, but I did have a fascination with words. And I think that that maybe tips me in the favor of being able to do this stuff. There's a guy I talked to one time named Richard Rubin, not to be confused with Rick Rubin. And he's a mnemonist and a very good one, who's very good with card magic that uses memory techniques. And he told me there's a period in American education where they got rid of phonology. And he thought that that's why a lot of people in a certain period have just really struggled to deal with memory techniques. Without doing any independent research myself, that theory kind of makes sense, because in my own teaching, I used to teach this to people and they just got it. They just understood this at a much higher level. And then all of a sudden there was this period where younger people or a certain group of people just — I don't get it. Like, you make numbers turn into sounds. And so, I don't know, like, I grew up at a time where we learned how to read by sounding things out. And there was this heavy emphasis on phonology. And I think that is a lot what memory techniques are, is a phonology thing. Anyway, as a kid, I remember very young knowing the word ridiculous and being fascinated with it and, like, really thinking about that word a lot. And ostensibly, I think I remember learning at one point when I was a kid, ramification. I remember learning ramification from Gremlins 2, the novelization, and asking my mom, what is this word? And she's like, let's look it up in the dictionary. But I don't know if that had to do with my memory or just my interest in sounds and words. But yeah, I guess.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: It's so great. Let's back up a little bit for the listenership and just talk about what a memory palace is, because it's such a fascinating concept. I learned about it in the early 80s from people who were interested in Giordano Bruno and stuff like that. The writing that I was reading at the time, they would bring up using memory palaces as this medieval memory technique. And they vaguely described it. And I tried to do it and had zero success with it. And reading your books and listening to what you have to say, I see why, and we can talk about that. But let's just talk about what it is and why it works.

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: Yeah, it's a very old technique that basically harnesses how that we naturally remember locations, or many of us do. And so what that means — a simple way to think about it is, the last time you moved, did you have to learn where your bedroom was? And you might have, but not with any massive effort. So if your mind just maps out locations quite quickly and easily, then you know where your kitchen is, therefore you know where your fridge is. And then inside the fridge is mustard. So you have a general idea where the mustard is relative to where the milk is. So that's how the memory palace works, is it harnesses that kind of general way that we know where things are. And the classic story of Simonides of Kos is that Simonides was giving a speech at a banquet or reciting some of his poetry, and long story short, he leaves the banquet hall and it gets crushed by an earthquake. And he's able to identify where all the guests are by where they were sitting. And so that became method of loci, or the method of locations. And so when we use a memory palace, that's essentially what we're doing, is we're taking something that we don't know but that we want to know, and we're sticking it in our fridge, or we're sticking it on our fridge like a magnet, and then we can refer back to it. Another part of this is the associations that we place there. So milk is kind of generic and vague, but if you think of Malcolm McDowell drinking milk from A Clockwork Orange in your fridge, well, that becomes kind of striking and weird. And so you have this dual chance to recall something, because now it's located, but it's also strange in that location, which is an effect that you create deliberately. And you can just take anything, as long as it's encoded in words or letters or numbers or symbols, and to a certain extent abstract shapes, then you can place it somewhere and then go back to it and recall it, provided that you encode it in a particular way by making it striking or unusual. Von Restorff effect is one of these words for this idea that if you make something unusual, you're much more likely to recognize it.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: So that's sort of two techniques, right? There's the one of placing various memories in a location we're already familiar with and kind of like leveraging location memory to help with memory of other facts. And then I believe it's what you call magnetic memory technique, right? We're making a striking visual image of the fact as well, or of the thing you're trying to remember as well. Is that correct?

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: Yeah, there's nuance on it though. And it's really cool, fascinating nuance, I think, because you're right. It is two techniques, and they actually had more than two names for this. So there's Ars Memorativa, which is the art of memory or the memory palace technique — it's usually referring to that. But then there's Ars Combinatoria, and that's the art of combination. And then there's, you know, like Ars Rerum, which has to do with the art of things, and Ars Verborum, which has to do with the art of the words, I guess, or verbatim sort of recall. Anyway, it gets super granular, and we've kind of lost that granularity in our mass media culture because people like Harry Lorayne and Tony Buzan never really outlined all of that stuff, at least not in those words. But yeah, the art of combination is literally like, how am I going to combine these images? So if I want to learn Advaita Vedanta, and I want to remember that term, well, the most famous advertising executive was Steve Vai — is a combination. It's not a memory palace, it's a combination, but the combination goes in the memory palace.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And where did you come up with that technique? Is that something you independently discovered and then found in some of the ancient stuff you've been looking into? Or did you just find it right in the source material?

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: Well, let's let Giordano Bruno answer it. Bruno said in one of his texts, he said, anyone who thinks long and hard enough about this will come to the same conclusion about how these techniques work as I did. So it's partly that you have to think about what you're reading in the text. But no, I didn't come up with any of this myself. I have added maybe a few things, but every time that I think that I added it, I find that it's in the text, in the tradition somewhere else. I've done exactly what Bruno said, is I just thought long and hard about it. But it's in Aristotle. De Memoria is what it's often called, but On Memory and Reminiscence, it's sometimes called. And if you read Aristotle on it, there's this really wild passage where he's talking about, okay, so you've got A, B, C, D, and E, and F, and G, and H. And if you can't remember something, well, instead of going back to A, go into F, and then go back to A. And this puzzles a lot of people. But to me, as a mnemonist, it makes complete sense what he's talking about. And I can unpack that if it's interesting.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah. What is he talking about?

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: Well, I have to say I'm speculating about what he's talking about, but I've read Richard Sorabji on Aristotle and memory, and Sorabji can't work it out. He really is puzzled by it. And so I thought long and hard about it, and this is what helped me the most, in addition to reading Bruno. Harry Lorayne, famous people like Tony Buzan, they also helped me, there's no doubt about it, but they never really quite got me to be able to memorize, for example, the Ribhu Gita extracts in Gary Weber's Evolving Beyond Thought. So in a memory palace, the problem is that we are now taught by memory competitors, and memory competitors use it for short-term gains. So they really just need the images that they place in the memory palaces to last for a very short period of time. But to be able to do a mantra, you need it to last for a very long time, perhaps forever, or for the duration of your life. What Aristotle is talking about when he says enter the alphabet in the middle and go back to the beginning, I believe he's talking about what we now call spaced repetition and primacy effect, recency effect, and serial positioning. So if you have a memory palace and the first part of your memory palace is A or 1, then the second part is B or 2. And if you always enter the memory palace from the beginning and you move to the end, you're going to give way too much emphasis to the first part, which is called primacy effect. And you'll remember that better than the middle part. The middle part will sink. So when he says enter the middle of the alphabet, he's talking — I believe very strongly, he's talking about giving primacy and recency to every part of your memory palace. And I later called that recall rehearsal. And it's a very specific way of using the memory palace. When you memorize, say, a mantra, I memorize that by first laying out the images in the memory palace. Then I recite it forward and I recite it backward. And then I go into the middle of it and I recite it from the middle to the beginning and the middle to the end. And then I skip all the stations. And the station skipping idea is serial positioning. And I got those ideas from Hermann Ebbinghaus, who wrote Über das Gedächtnis in German, which is about memory. And it's kind of just thinking about it and then applying it. And I've just found, and I've seen it replicated many, many times, that you can get things into longer-term memory much, much faster by following those patterns. And it's basically how Anki works. And Anki, for people who don't know, that is a spaced repetition software. Anki is trying to produce primacy and recency effects by using an algorithm to get you to expose yourself to the information in order to prompt long-term retention. The only reason I don't use Anki myself is that I just don't find that it's nearly as effective as manually entering the alphabet in the middle, as Aristotle seems to say.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Well, this is where I can start to really confirm personally what you're saying. As I said, I learned about memory palaces in the 80s as part of being interested in ritual magic and chaos magic. They didn't call it chaos magic back then, but what we would now recognize as chaos magic. And they were talking about Bruno and memory palaces. And it just seemed like the coolest thing in the world. And I wanted to do it. But what I didn't understand is that you have to use a place you already know. I thought, oh, I've got to kind of like imagine a palace with all these rooms and then put memories in those rooms. Which of course, when you do it that way, which is incorrect, you're not using an already existing memory and leveraging that to help you memorize. You're just making more work for yourself. So it didn't catch on way back then. But when I started working with your material and used just in general what you're calling recall rehearsal — starting in the middle, going forward, going backwards, changing the order, doing every other one, doing every other one backwards, stuff like that — that was one of the most interesting experiences I've had in a long time. It sounds maybe ridiculous to say so, but it really was like the feeling of getting locked in on this very complex Sanskrit text, just getting completely locked in. Like, I've got this. It's in my mind. You could feel it like kind of burrowing into your mind, just being installed. It was really interesting. And all I'm talking about is going forwards and backwards and, you know, out of order and in a different order and stuff like that. But the subjective experience was like, whoa, you know, that's there now. And so the recall rehearsal, I feel, ended up being maybe the most striking when learning to do this. So I can really say that that helped tremendously and also was just cool. I was like, I've never felt something like that in my mind before. To do that on such a big level all at once. Powerful stuff.

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: It really is quite something. And I don't know why that it disappeared at some point, other than that memory competitors don't need it, but they just sort of dominated the publication market around this for quite some time. And it's not that unusual in music to practice a scale backwards, you know, or to know where the third degree of a scale is and start from the middle. It seems so unusual when we talk about doing this with a text, but it's not in music, not at all, far from it. And there may be other performance arts where you would also investigate or learn a move, like in — I don't know this for a fact, but it would make sense to me to learn certain moves by also breaking them apart, at least mentally rotating them backwards, and so on.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: Yeah, in martial arts, we have done that before. It's interesting because as a kid, I was very excited about memorizing poems and memorizing song lyrics and stuff like that, and did that a lot. I spent a lot of time reciting, but that was just from rote. And as an adult meditation practitioner and spiritual practitioner, I learned a lot of long Sanskrit texts, again, by rote. So I have a lot of experience of what it's like, the joy for me, actually deep satisfaction, of just sitting down and reciting this stuff. I love that as a practice, focusing on it, reciting it from memory. But the rote version is real different than doing it with these techniques like a memory palace and recall rehearsal. That's why it was so surprising, because I felt like, well, I've done a lot of this before, this will just make it a little easier. And really, it made it shockingly easier. So I was very grateful for that. So when you've seen people do this kind of work, they're following your techniques or learning to memorize stuff, what are some typical outcomes for this? How do you see this in general? And this is, of course, anecdotally, but you do have a large group of students, I imagine. How do you see this really affecting people in sort of a long-term way or a positive way?

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: To me, this is the great mystery, because it is true, it's anecdotal, and I have all kinds of testimonials. And sometimes I've been able to test those, actually. And sometimes those tests are not as sparkling as one would want, because people get quite excited, then you say, okay, let's get on a call and show me, and then they stumble. But the beauty of it is — and then they get embarrassed. And if this is like, believe me, I've stumbled. Man, I never know if it's going to work when I open my mouth, but it does often enough. More often enough to prove its own point, at least in my practice. But I have to admit that it could be that I did it all by rote. So that's part of the problem with this teaching, is that if people are skeptical, they're right to be skeptical. But I think that the skepticism is the tool. I mean, I like this because it sounds fun, but I don't know if it's actually a good thing. But I like to think of myself as a true skeptic, which is to say that as long as it's not some substance that I have to take or some device that I have to wear on my head or whatever, I like to really test things out. And I learned a hard lesson in life, which is that I've rejected a lot of stuff offhand, and it was like, there's no there there. But then when I actually took on things like memorizing mantras, I was like, wow, there is something here, actually. So I like to test as much as I can. And that's the thing that I throw to people. And I say this little fancy thing. There's thousands of years of tradition. There are decades of memory competitor records and more science than anyone has time to read. I mean, that's my marketing shtick. But it's true. And it doesn't matter what I say. It's independently confirmed over and over and over again. There are other schmucks with stuff to sell who do this like I do. And maybe I'm the only one who actually embraces the used car salesman personality, but I love it. It's the greatest insult that I ever received. Because if I had the cure for cancer, I hope I would scream this loud. Because it just works, and it doesn't rely on me. It's not my opinion, unless I'm the only one — this solipsism is real. I think that the challenge here is just getting people to test their own skepticism and do it. And the skepticism thing — Lynne Kelly, she's amazing. She wrote The Knowledge Gene most recently, The Memory Code, Memory Craft. She's actually a member of the Australian Skeptic Society. She was skeptical of it all. But lo and behold, she winds up getting the Order of Australia largely on the strength of her writing about memory, I think, or at least that contributed to it. And she's performed really well at memory competitions, but she didn't believe it for a second when she first heard about it, because it sounds so wild and outlandish, but it just isn't. It's the real magic. It is actual magic that works.

transcript.speaker: Michael Taft
transcript.text: And as you know, I'm a meditation teacher. And one of the things that I've seen is that traditionally, and some of these traditions are preserved, this kind of sit down and recite stuff is a big part of practice. I think often in the West, we've imported a lot of these practices and then kind of unbundled them from their context. And so we're just using pieces of practice rather than whole practice systems. And I think in a lot of ways, that's really cool. Some of this stuff works really well unbundled. But what we've decided when we do that unbundling, what we've decided to kind of like leave by the side of the road for the garbage man to pick up often is something that is really helpful, cool, interesting, powerful, beautiful, let alone, you know, perhaps necessary. But a lot of it, when you get into the deep practice context, turns out to be kind of awesome. And one of them, a big one, is this long recitation stuff, sitting down and doing aloud or just in your mind, but often aloud, doing a stotram, you know, where it's like, okay, this is seven solid minutes, ten solid minutes of very difficult Sanskrit that you just sit down and recite, and maybe recite it over and over. And this is considered to be a meditation technique that is very powerful. And years ago, I learned that that really does get you highly concentrated. It can really change your mood. It can really get you, of course, ready for silent meditation with no recitation. But also in and of itself, it's just an enjoyable, beautiful practice that usually, if you're doing it in a context, clicks together, puzzle piece fits with all the other stuff you're doing in that tradition in a really cool way. And so I, years ago, found that I like doing it. But I see that very few traditions do that in the West now. Some do. If you stick with a tradition that's kind of more conservative, there's going to be a lot of that, very often translated into English, which is another interesting question. But what we've got here is something that I think really just makes it so much easier to do, makes it more enjoyable. It's not just a party trick. I think a really interesting point you made is that this isn't just memorizing digits of pi, which is an amazing feat, and the fact that people can do that is great, but it's not just a party trick or like a magic trick, right? This is meaningful, powerful, beautiful, rich text that ties into your overall meditation practice, spiritual practice, whatever. The fact that this makes it so much easier to learn and so much quicker and also in a funny way richer — and I want to ask some questions about that richer point. But this fact just to me was — I got really excited about it, as I do sometimes, and started talking to people about it and working with students on it. In any case, the fact that it makes it so much more accessible, I just think is wonderful. And I'm curious, like for you, how do you use it? I know you memorized an Advaita Vedanta text. When you're using that to actually practice meditation, or as a meditative practice or as a spiritual practice, how do you do that?

transcript.speaker: Anthony Metivier
transcript.text: Well, I was very blessed that a friend kind of called me on my BS at one point. He asked me, have you ever memorized any mantras? And I was like, no, I'm a militant atheist, what would I be bothering with any of that stuff? I don't know if it's true or not, but he put it in this very kind way. He's like, well, you know, there's this guy Gary Weber who also basically needed to have a secular approach to these things, and he wound up memorizing all this Sanskrit. And it was kind of like a movie where the call to adventure happens, you know — here, young squire, this is the path. And so I immediately went home and ordered this book, Happiness Beyond Thought, and I basically just did what Happiness Beyond Thought says. And Dr. Weber is very, very good, and I hope that people read him as closely as I tried to read him. I'm sure I've missed details, but he says one thing that leapt out at me immediately in Happiness Beyond Thought. He said, do not try to reproduce anyone else's journey. That to me is the greatest gift ever, right? That's very good advice. Nonetheless, I mean, I still tried to reproduce what he's saying there as closely as possible, but not making that error of trying to be Dr. Weber, you know, because his story is quite a big claim, right? That all thoughts switched off like blowing out a candle. And I just thought, no, this is nonsense, but I'm going to try. Like, this is the sort of principle of being the true skeptic. So what it is, is I first had to memorize the text. And what I first did was just the neti neti. I memorized neti neti, and then I memorized Kirtan Kriya, like sat nam. What's the Sanskrit text within Happiness Beyond Thought? I have the book over there on the shelf, so I could look it up, but I don't want to. Happiness Beyond Thought has Nirvana Shatakam, and it has Upadesa Saram, and it has part of the Bhagavad Gita. And I don't distinctly recall if those passages of the Bhagavad Gita are Song Celestial, but in a different book that he has called Dancing Beyond Thought, he's essentially got Song Celestial. I think it's 66 verses, something like that. But at that time when I started, I just started with neti neti and sat nam. And it was only when Evolving Beyond Thought came out that I read that. And then I memorized the Ribhu Gita extracts in there, which is 32 of them. And it didn't take me very long to memorize them. I don't know why I didn't immediately do the Sanskrit that's in Happiness Beyond Thought, but I circled back to it after I finished the Ribhu Gita extracts. So basically, the practice is a little bit of asana stuff, like really simple baby pose, I think you call it, touching your toes, that kind of stuff, just to get in your body a little bit, out of your head. And then I do a little bit of breathing. And then he has this thing called number skipping, where you count from one to ten. And it's kind of like skipping stations in a memory palace. You count from one to ten, but you suppress two and you suppress four. And then when you come back down, you suppress the odd numbers. Very challenging, but very good for reaching persistent non-symbolic experience or, quote unquote, having no thoughts, because you're actually forcing yourself to not think of the red cat that is the number two, or wherever you are in the sequence. transcript.text: Yeah, this is always a kind of personal decision. From an I'm-a-teacher-do-this kind of perspective, what I would recommend for people is to have as many memory palaces as possible and use them. And the reason why is because it'll expand your skills and it'll give you interleaving effects. And interleaving is a very specific thing that promotes better memory. It's literally, you know, abandoning this to go and do that. And that can actually help with memory. So when I memorized these pieces very quickly, part of the reason I was able to do it quickly in terms of remembering it long-term is because I interleaved it. I deliberately moved from one memory palace to the other so that I could do them all at once, so to speak. And it didn't slow me down. It's not better to just focus on one until it's done. That actually can lead to topic exhaustion. So by memorizing more than one thing at once and having multiple memory palaces to enable you to do that, I think you get more bang for your buck at the end of the day. And the risk of using the same place over and over again is what memory competitors call ghosting, or sometimes called in memory science the ugly sister effect. And that's in a book called Mnemonology, which is just a wild ride into memory science if anybody wants to read it. If you memorize a deck of cards in one memory palace and then you shuffle it and you memorize a new order, layering it onto the same location, the previous images will either interfere, or when you do recall, you can miscall the cards because you just had a set there.
